**Tests**: `entityFormatting.test.ts` gained two tests after the existing relation-matching tests: one confirming both `"1500"` and `"1,500"` match a `total: 1500` record while `"9999"` doesn't, and one confirming the default `lang` ("en") doesn't throw when omitted. `codegen.test.ts` gained the equivalent test against the real generated `matchesSearch`, extracted alone (the number branch needs none of the relation helpers the file's existing relation test depends on).

**A real regression surfaced and fixed along the way**: adding the new `lang` parameter broke `GlobalSearchPanel.test.ts`'s own regex-extraction tests for `runSearch`/`handleShowAll` -- exactly the standing "a new dependency/param on an existing handler breaks its regex-extraction tests, grep for all of them" lesson from rounds 356-407. Two `not ok` failures (`ReferenceError: lang is not defined`) surfaced on the first full `@forge/web` run; found and updated all four `new Function(...)` extraction blocks in that file (three for `runSearch`, one for `handleShowAll`) to add `"lang"` to the parameter list and `"en"` as the matching argument, mirroring every other mocked dependency already there.

**Regression-proof**: backed up all four changed implementation files (`entityFormatting.ts`, `EntityPanel.tsx`, `GlobalSearchPanel.tsx`, `codegen.ts`) to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted all four to HEAD (keeping the updated test files). The predicted failure occurred exactly: 802 passed, 2 failed -- the two new `entityFormatting.test.ts` tests (the `GlobalSearchPanel.test.ts` extraction tests stayed green on revert too, since an unused extra mock parameter is harmless when the reverted handler never references it). Restored all four files from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q` on each, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/web`/`@forge/api` suites clean.

Full suite green: **804 tests** in `@forge/web` (+2), **389 tests** in `@forge/api` (+1), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/db`, `@forge/shared`, and `@forge/spec-engine` (untouched by the final fix -- the `packages/shared` validation attempt was fully reverted, not landed) stayed at their round-414 counts. Pushed as commit `3cc9e41`.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. The `matchesSearch` number-formatting gap (round 408's own original candidate) is closed in both the live preview and the exported app. The `relationTo`-validation idea explored and reverted this round is **not** a bug and must not be re-attempted without a way to distinguish an intentional "entity may not exist yet" placeholder (round 59-60's own established design) from a genuine AI-generated mismatch -- noted here so a future round doesn't re-discover and re-attempt the same reverted approach. Everything else still open from rounds 378-414 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 416: seeding a required relation could throw a real FK violation, silently masked by the time QA ran

**The survey**: a fresh Explore general-survey was explicitly told to discount all five now-closed families (tolerant-listing completeness, staleness/race guards, migration-diff one-step-back blindness, asymmetric new-branch coverage, and matchesSearch display-value mismatches) and not to re-propose the relationTo-validation idea round 415 had just tested and reverted. It surfaced a candidate in `packages/db/src/seed.ts`/`apps/api/src/pipeline.ts` whose own root cause had actually been found and explicitly, honestly deferred in an early self-review, long before the per-round numbering in this log began -- confirmed by grepping `docs/roadmap.md` for "guaranteed insert order": that entry already named the exact gap ("required relation fields seeded with an unverified id=1 guess that can violate a real FK constraint... properly fixing... needs a real design decision (topological seed ordering)... noted honestly for a future round instead of rushed") and explicitly left it open, unreachable through the built-in domain library (every built-in relation field is `required: false`) and therefore invisible except through a real AI-generated or refined spec.

**Independent verification**: read `seed.ts`'s `seedValueFor` (the `"relation"` case, confirmed its own comment says exactly this: "Best-effort guess (row 1) when the field is required; there's no guaranteed insert order across entities yet"). Read `pipeline.ts`'s Seed Data step (lines ~355-394) and confirmed `entitiesToSeed` is a plain `.filter()` over `nextSpec.entities`, preserving the spec's own array order with no dependency sort anywhere (grepped both files for `sort(` -- zero hits) -- and confirmed the failed-seed branch (`seedErrors.length > 0`) yields a `status: "failed"` event but has no `return` after it, unlike the QA step a few lines below which does `return` on `!qa.allPassed`, so a seeding failure here never actually stops the build. Read `runQaChecks` (lines 170-220) and confirmed its required-field smoke test builds a full `validRecord` via `generateSeedRecords(entity, 1)[0]` (which includes the SAME guessed `customerId: 1` for any OTHER required field under test) and only deletes the one field currently being tested -- so testing a required relation field itself (deleting it entirely) only ever exercises the "missing field" validation path, never a real FK-constrained insert; and testing a *different* required field on the same entity inserts a record that still carries the guessed relation id, which only succeeds if the target already has real rows. Traced the concrete failure end-to-end: a spec listing `[Invoice, Customer]` with `Invoice.customerId` a required relation to `Customer` makes every one of Invoice's own seed inserts throw a real `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed` (Customer has zero rows when Invoice is processed first) -- caught into `seedErrors`, reported as a failed Seed Data step, but the pipeline continues; `Customer` is then seeded successfully in its own later turn in the same loop; by the time QA runs, Customer's row 1 genuinely exists, so the same guessed id now succeeds there too, masking that `Invoice`'s table is left with zero rows while every sibling entity has its usual two -- the one thing seeding exists to prevent (`generateSeedRecords`'s own doc-comment: "a freshly built app never opens to an empty, unconvincing table"), silently failing for the entirely ordinary case of a required relation. Reproduced the whole chain directly via a real `runBuildPipeline` run before writing the fix, confirming the Seed Data step reports `"failed"` and `Invoice` ends up with 0 rows. Confirmed `codegen.ts` has no seed-data concept at all (grepped for "seed" and for `generateSeedRecords`/`seedValueFor` -- zero hits), so no porting was needed.

**The fix**: added `orderForSeeding` to `packages/db/src/seed.ts` -- a plain topological sort of a seed batch by required-relation target (an entity depends on every OTHER entity in the same batch that one of its own required relation fields points at, deduplicated per target so multiple required fields pointing at the same entity don't inflate the dependency count), falling back to the given relative order for anything left unresolved in a cycle (including a self-relation, e.g. `Employee.managerId -> Employee`, deliberately left exactly as unaddressed as before -- this generator has no way to seed "before itself"). Wired into `pipeline.ts`: `entitiesToSeed` is now `orderForSeeding(nextSpec.entities.filter(...))` instead of the bare filter. Updated `seedValueFor`'s own comment to describe the new, still-honest state (correct for the ordinary case now; still just a guess for a relation to an entity with pre-existing rows from an earlier build, a self-relation, or a genuine cycle).

**Tests**: `packages/db/src/seed.test.ts` gained five tests for `orderForSeeding` directly: reorders `[Invoice, Customer]` to put `Customer` first; leaves unrelated entities in their original relative order; does NOT reorder for an *optional* relation (only a required one actually needs a real row to point at); falls back to the original order instead of looping forever on a genuine two-entity cycle; and doesn't loop forever on a self-relation. `apps/api/src/pipeline.test.ts` gained one full end-to-end test via the real `runBuildPipeline`, placed directly after the existing re-seeding-retry test: the `[Invoice, Customer]` spec now seeds both tables with real rows, the Seed Data step reports success (not failed), and QA still passes -- using `events.find((e) => e.agent === "X" && e.status !== "running")` to grab the terminal event rather than the step's own leading "running" event, a minor test-writing gotcha caught and fixed before this round's own regression-proof cycle (not a product bug).

**Regression-proof**: backed up all three changed implementation files (`packages/db/src/seed.ts`, `packages/db/src/index.ts`, `apps/api/src/pipeline.ts`) to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted all three to HEAD (keeping the updated test files). The predicted failures occurred exactly: `@forge/db` crashed at module load (`seed.test.ts`'s own `import { orderForSeeding } from "./seed.js"` naming an export that no longer existed -- a module-load crash, this project's own established strong-confirmation signal), and `@forge/api` showed the new pipeline test failing with the Seed Data step reporting `"failed"` instead of `"success"`, the exact real bug. Restored all three files from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q` on each, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/db`/`@forge/api` suites clean.

Full suite green: **118 tests** in `@forge/db` (+5), **390 tests** in `@forge/api` (+1), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/web`, `@forge/shared`, and `@forge/spec-engine` (untouched, no re-run needed) stayed at their round-415 counts. Pushed as commit `7f36351`.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. It closes a gap that was honestly identified and deliberately deferred in an early self-review (predating this log's per-round numbering) rather than rushed at the time -- confirming the standing "a candidate a previous round identified but didn't implement is still 'ready'" lesson holds even across that much distance, once independently re-verified fresh rather than taken on faith. The residual self-relation and genuine-cycle cases remain exactly as unaddressed as documented, a deliberate scope boundary, not a bug. Everything else still open from rounds 378-415 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 417: an entity table sorted an enum column by its raw stored code, not the translated label shown on screen

**The survey**: a fresh Explore general-survey was told to discount all six now-closed families (tolerant-listing completeness, staleness/race guards, migration-diff one-step-back blindness, asymmetric new-branch coverage, matchesSearch display-value mismatches, and seed dependency ordering) and not to re-propose the relationTo-validation idea round 415 reverted. It found that `resolveSortValue` (in both `apps/web/src/entityFormatting.ts` and its plain-JS duplicate in `apps/api/src/codegen.ts`) only special-cased `relation` fields for display-based sorting -- an `enum` field fell straight through to raw-value sorting, even though the table cell render and `matchesSearch` both already resolve an enum value through `field.enumLabels` before showing or matching it.

**Independent verification**: read both copies of `resolveSortValue` directly and confirmed the old top-level guard (`if (!fields || !allEntities || !relatedRecords) return value;` in `entityFormatting.ts`; the analogous `fields && relatedRecords` ternary one level up in `codegen.ts`'s `sortRecordsMulti`) only ever branched on `field.type === "relation"`, with no `enum` case at all -- so clicking an enum column's header sorted `"P1"`/`"P3"` lexically instead of by whatever label (`"Low"`/`"High"`) was actually on screen. Confirmed this was reachable in practice (not just a hypothetical): an enum field is a normal, common field type, and sorting is wired up on every entity table regardless of field type.

**The fix**: rewrote `resolveSortValue` in `entityFormatting.ts` to check `field?.type === "enum"` first and return `field.enumLabels?.[String(value)] ?? value` (falling back to the raw value when a value has no `enumLabels` entry, rather than sorting by `undefined`), splitting the old single top-level guard into per-branch checks so the enum case only needs `fields`, not `allEntities`/`relatedRecords`. Mirrored the same change in `codegen.ts`'s plain-JS `resolveSortValue`.

While verifying the `codegen.ts` side with a new test, found a second, real sub-bug: `codegen.ts`'s own `sortRecordsMulti` had a stale outer guard (`fields && relatedRecords ? compareValues(resolveSortValue(...)) : compareValues(a[field], b[field])`) that skipped calling `resolveSortValue` entirely unless BOTH `fields` AND `relatedRecords` were truthy -- a leftover from when `resolveSortValue` only ever needed both (for the relation case). Traced the real call site (the exported app's `EntityView` component, `visibleRecords`'s `useMemo`) and confirmed `relatedRecords` is a `useState({})`-initialized value there, so it is never actually falsy in production -- meaning this guard was never reachable with a falsy value at the one real call site, not a production bug by itself. Fixed it anyway to remove the architectural drift: removed the ternary so `resolveSortValue` is called unconditionally, exactly matching `entityFormatting.ts`'s own `sortRecordsMulti`, which has never had such a guard. `resolveSortValue` itself was made safe for a missing `fields`/`relatedRecords` (`fields?.find(...)`, and the relation branch returns the raw value when `relatedRecords` is falsy) so this is a pure simplification, not a behavior change for any existing caller.

**Tests**: `apps/web/src/entityFormatting.test.ts` gained three tests: `sortRecords` sorts by an enum's label (not the raw code); `sortRecords` falls back to the raw value when a value has no `enumLabels` entry; `sortRecordsMulti` resolves an enum key to its label too, composing correctly with a non-enum tiebreaker key. `apps/api/src/codegen.test.ts` gained one test for the exported `EntityView`'s `sortRecordsMulti`, extracting `compareValues`/`resolveSortValue`/`sortRecordsMulti` from the generated output via the established regex-extraction convention. Writing that test surfaced a second, pre-existing regex-extraction test (round-177's "sorts by several fields in priority order" test) that only extracted `compareValues` and `sortRecordsMulti` -- removing the stale guard made that test's `sortRecordsMulti` call `resolveSortValue`, which wasn't in scope in that test's own `new Function(...)` call, so it was updated to also extract and include `resolveSortValueSrc`, per this project's own standing regex-extraction-test convention (a changed function's dependency list can break other files' `new Function(...)` test assemblies, not just its own co-located test).

**Regression-proof**: backed up both changed implementation files (`apps/web/src/entityFormatting.ts`, `apps/api/src/codegen.ts`) to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted both to HEAD (keeping the updated test files). The predicted failures occurred exactly: `@forge/api` showed the new enum-sort test failing (1 failure, everything else green); `@forge/web` showed exactly the two label-resolution tests failing (the third, fallback-behavior test correctly stayed green, since that path is unaffected by the fix). Restored both files from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q` on each, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/web`/`@forge/api` suites clean.

Full suite green: **391 tests** in `@forge/api` (+1), **807 tests** in `@forge/web` (+3), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/db`, `@forge/shared`, and `@forge/spec-engine` (untouched, no re-run needed) stayed at their round-416 counts. Pushed as commit `ff7732d`.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. The enum-sort/display mismatch joins the closed matchesSearch-display-mismatch family (round 415) as a sibling gap in the same general shape -- a value's sort/search logic lagging behind its own display logic -- now fully closed across number, relation, and enum field types. The `sortRecordsMulti` guard cleanup in `codegen.ts` is a real architectural fix (closing a latent gap that would have mattered had `relatedRecords` ever been falsy at a future call site) even though it wasn't reachable as a bug through today's one real call site. Everything else still open from rounds 378-416 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 418: a whole entity removed then re-added under the same name never got its new fields migrated, surfacing as a raw SQLite crash

**The survey**: a fresh Explore general-survey was given an explicit, long denylist covering all ~70+ closed items and both deliberately-deferred candidates (wakeRetry.ts idempotency, round 387; ProductSpecSchema relationTo validation, round 415), and told to look at genuinely unexplored territory. It found `packages/db/src/migrate.ts`'s `diffAndMigrate`, in the `!prevEntity` branch (the top of the per-entity loop, lines 173-177): when an entity name has no match in `previousSpec`, the function unconditionally treats it as brand-new -- runs `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and `return`s immediately, without ever entering the per-field diff loop a few lines below that already handles new/changed columns for an *existing* entity.

**Independent verification**: confirmed `previousSpec` at the one real call site (`apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts:662`, `previousSpec: project.spec`) is always just the single spec immediately before this one refine turn, never a cumulative history of every entity that ever existed in the project. So an entity removed on refine B and re-added under the *same name* on a later refine C has no `prevEntity` when C's own `diffAndMigrate` call runs (B's spec, the `previousSpec` for that call, doesn't have it) -- but because migrations are additive-only (this file's own doc-comment, and round 389's deleteProject-table-orphan fix both confirm tables are never dropped), the *physical* table from the entity's original build still exists. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` against an existing table is a silent no-op, `new_table` is wrongly reported even though nothing happened, and the field loop that would otherwise `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` for whatever the re-added entity's fields now need never runs at all. Reproduced directly: build A has `Courier{name}`; refine B removes `Courier`; refine C re-adds `Courier{name, phone}`. After C, `PRAGMA table_info` on the live table showed only `name` -- `phone` was never added. The very next `insertRecord`/`updateRecord` call supplying a `phone` value throws a raw, unhandled SQLite `no such column: phone` error -- surfacing as a 500, or routing into the paid Debug-Agent repair path in `pipeline.ts`, for the entirely ordinary case of "remove an entity, then bring it back."

Confirmed this is NOT the same gap as round 413's closed "field removed and re-added on the same still-existing entity" fix: that fix's `physicalColumnShape` stale-column check only ever runs inside the field loop, which is reached when `prevEntity` is truthy (the entity itself was never removed) -- the whole-*entity*-level `!prevEntity` branch sits one level above that loop and `return`s before physicalColumnShape is ever consulted for a reused entity, structurally untouched by round 413's fix. Grepped `docs/roadmap.md` for "entity removed"/"re-added"/"readd"/"table reuse"/"stale table" -- the only entity-removal-related closed item is round 389 (orphaning a table on whole-*project* deletion, an unrelated cleanup concern).

**The fix**: `diffAndMigrate` now checks whether the table *physically* exists (via `existingColumns(db, table).size === 0`, computed once and reused) rather than relying solely on whether `prevEntity` is truthy, before taking the `new_table` shortcut. When the table already exists despite no `prevEntity` matching, it falls through to the same per-field diff loop an ordinary existing entity already uses, with `prevFieldsByName` built from an empty array when there's no `prevEntity` to source it from -- so every field on the reused entity takes the same "reused column, compare against physical reality" path `physicalColumnShape` already provides for a single reused *field* (round 413). A benign reuse (identical shape to before removal) stays silent, exactly as before; a genuine gap (a new or changed field) is reported as `new_column`/`type_changed`/`relation_target_changed`/`relation_missing_fk` and its column is actually added via `ALTER TABLE`, closing the crash.

One scoped-out side effect, left deliberately unaddressed: `pipeline.ts`'s Seed Data step only auto-seeds sample records for entities reported as `new_table` with zero existing rows (round 416's `orderForSeeding`, gated on `newEntityNames`). A re-added entity is no longer reported as `new_table` (it now reports `new_column` per field, correctly), so if it happens to have zero rows at the moment of re-adding, it will no longer get auto-seeded sample data the way it accidentally did before this fix (when the bug mislabeled it `new_table`). Deliberately not changed this round: broadening the seeding gate to "any entity with zero rows" would also auto-reseed an *existing*, never-removed entity a user intentionally bulk-deleted all rows from -- a worse, unrelated regression. This is a narrow, honest cosmetic gap (an empty table instead of sample rows after a specific remove-then-re-add-while-empty sequence), not a crash, and not addressed here.

**Tests**: `packages/db/src/migrate.test.ts` gained two tests: the re-added entity with an extra field actually gets the new column added (and a real `insertRecord` using it succeeds, not just a reported change), and the benign twin -- a re-added entity with identical fields reports no `new_table` and no spurious `type_changed`.

**Regression-proof**: backed up `packages/db/src/migrate.ts` to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted it to HEAD (keeping the updated test file). The predicted failures occurred exactly: both new tests failed (`@forge/db` 118/120), everything else green. Restored from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q`, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/db`/`@forge/api` suites clean (`@forge/api` re-run since it consumes `diffAndMigrate`'s output in `pipeline.ts`).

Full suite green: **120 tests** in `@forge/db` (+2), **391 tests** in `@forge/api` (unchanged -- no API-level test needed; the bug and fix are entirely inside `migrate.ts`), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/web`, `@forge/shared`, and `@forge/spec-engine` (untouched, no re-run needed) stayed at their round-417 counts. Pushed as commit `8e92b06`.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. It closes the sibling gap to round 413's field-level stale-reuse fix, at the entity level instead of the field level -- the same "previousSpec is only ever one step back" blindness, applying one level higher than where it was first found. The Seed Data auto-seeding gap for a re-added-while-empty entity is a deliberately scoped-out, honest, low-severity gap, not a bug to revisit without a materially different angle (e.g. an explicit "this table is empty AND the table's SQL schema was just extended this diff" signal, which doesn't exist today). Everything else still open from rounds 378-417 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 419: renaming a Time Machine checkpoint silently reclassified it as the wrong build/refine type

**The survey**: a fresh Explore general-survey was given an explicit denylist covering all closed families (including round 418's entity-level migration-reuse fix) and told to look at structurally different territory, away from the "previousSpec one-step-back blindness" and "display-vs-stored-value" families that dominated recent rounds. It found `getCheckpointType` (`apps/web/src/checkpointDiff.ts`) classifying a checkpoint as `"build"` vs `"refine"` purely by re-parsing its own *label* on every read (`label.startsWith("Refine:") || label.startsWith("שיפור:")`), while `CheckpointLabelEditor.tsx` (round 209) lets a user freely rename any checkpoint's label to arbitrary text -- its own advertised use case being exactly "give an important one a name that's actually memorable."

**Independent verification**: confirmed `CheckpointSchema` (`packages/shared/src/index.ts`) had no field at all besides `label` that could tell build from refine -- no `kind`/`type` column anywhere, and `packages/db/src/checkpoints.ts`'s own table schema (`id, projectId, label, spec_json, createdAt`) confirmed the same at the storage layer. Confirmed `renameCheckpoint` places zero restriction on the new label (no prefix requirement) and its own test (`checkpoints.test.ts`) already renames `"Initial build"` to `"before the pricing overhaul"` as the intended, documented use case. Traced the concrete failure: a refine checkpoint labeled `"Refine: add invoice tracking"`, renamed to anything not starting with `"Refine:"`/`"שיפור:"`, is reclassified as `"build"` by `getCheckpointType` on its very next read -- HistoryPanel's build/refine filter dropdown then wrongly hides it under "Refines only" and wrongly shows it under "Initial build". The reverse (a build renamed to text that happens to start with `"Refine:"`) is also possible, though less likely in practice. Grepped `docs/roadmap.md` for "getCheckpointType"/"rename"/"classification" -- round 183 (added the heuristic) and round 209 (added rename) never tested the interaction between the two, and no later round documents this as found, deferred, or rejected. Confirmed it isn't a design decision: nothing suggests the label-prefix classification was ever meant to survive the very rename feature the product later added.

**The fix**: `CheckpointSchema` gained a `kind: z.enum(["build", "refine"])` field, set once at checkpoint creation and never re-derived from `label` again. `apps/api/src/pipeline.ts`'s one `insertCheckpoint` call (inside `runBuildPipeline`) now passes `kind: previousSpec ? "refine" : "build"` -- `previousSpec` is already the one unambiguous signal distinguishing /build from /refine at the only two call sites that ever set `changeLabel` (`routes/projects.ts`'s `/build` and `/refine` routes), so no new parameter had to be threaded through either route. `packages/db/src/checkpoints.ts`'s `ensureCheckpointsTable` adds the new `kind` column to the real `checkpoints` table (`ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN kind TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'build'`, additive-only, the same discipline `migrate.ts` uses everywhere else) and runs a one-time `UPDATE` backfilling `kind = 'refine'` for every pre-existing row whose label still matches the old prefix heuristic -- the best recoverable answer for data written before this column existed; a checkpoint already renamed away from its original prefix *before* this migration ever runs can't be recovered correctly by that backfill, an honest, unavoidable limit of reconstructing history from the only signal that ever existed for it. `getCheckpointType` now just returns `checkpoint.kind` directly. `renameCheckpoint` was already correct by construction (its own `UPDATE` only ever touches `label`) and needed no code change, just a doc-comment making that guarantee explicit.

**Tests**: `packages/db/src/checkpoints.test.ts` gained two tests: renaming a checkpoint to text with no "Refine:" prefix at all leaves its `kind` unchanged (both the in-memory return value and a fresh re-read from storage), and a dedicated migration test standing in for a pre-existing table (manually created in the old, column-less shape, with rows in both English and Hebrew, build and refine) that confirms `ensureCheckpointsTable` adds the column and backfills every row correctly, and that re-running it a second time (every app startup) is a safe no-op that doesn't re-derive or disturb an already-backfilled value. `apps/web/src/checkpointDiff.test.ts` gained a regression test proving `getCheckpointType` keeps reading a renamed refine checkpoint as `"refine"` (and a build renamed to coincidentally "Refine:"-prefixed text as `"build"`), plus updated every existing `getCheckpointType`/`filterCheckpointsByType` test and fixture to pass `kind` explicitly now that it's no longer derivable from the label alone. `apps/api/src/pipeline.test.ts` gained an integration-level test driving a real build then a real refine through `runBuildPipeline` and confirming the two resulting checkpoints land with `kind: "build"` and `kind: "refine"` respectively -- verifying the actual wiring (the `previousSpec ? "refine" : "build"` ternary), not just the isolated `insertCheckpoint`/`getCheckpointType` unit behavior. `HistoryPanel.test.ts` and `CheckpointLabelEditor.test.ts`'s own `Checkpoint` fixtures were updated to satisfy the now-required `kind` field.

**Regression-proof**: backed up all four changed implementation files (`packages/shared/src/index.ts`, `packages/db/src/checkpoints.ts`, `apps/api/src/pipeline.ts`, `apps/web/src/checkpointDiff.ts`) to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted all four to HEAD (keeping every updated test file). The predicted failures occurred exactly across all three affected workspaces: `@forge/db` showed precisely the two new tests failing (120/122); `@forge/web` showed precisely the one new rename-immunity test failing (32/33 in `checkpointDiff.test.ts` alone); `@forge/api` showed precisely the new build/refine integration test failing (391/392). Restored all four files from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q` on each, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/db`/`@forge/api`/`@forge/web` suites clean.

Full suite green: **122 tests** in `@forge/db` (+2), **392 tests** in `@forge/api` (+1), **808 tests** in `@forge/web` (+1), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/shared` (schema-only change, no new test needed) and `@forge/spec-engine` (untouched) stayed at their round-418 counts. Pushed as commit `50c2b87` + roadmap entry to follow.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. It's a structurally different bug-class from the migration-reuse family (rounds 413/414/418) and the display-vs-stored-value family (round 415/417): a value computed from a user-editable field being treated as if it were immutable, with no persisted field actually backing the distinction until now. The Seed Data gap from round 418 and the other open small candidates remain open and unchanged.

### Round 420: deleting a single Time Machine checkpoint could leave a real data table permanently orphaned once the project itself was later deleted

**The survey**: a fresh Explore general-survey was given an explicit denylist covering all closed families, told not to re-propose round 419's own checkpoint/label case, but to apply its general lesson (a value re-derived live from a user-editable field is fragile once an edit feature exists for that field) when looking elsewhere. It found `deleteProject` (`packages/db/src/projects.ts`) relies on `listAllCheckpointedEntityNames` (`packages/db/src/checkpoints.ts`) to find every entity a project's spec ever contained, so it can drop tables for entities since removed from the spec (`migrate.ts`'s migrations are additive-only and never drop these tables themselves -- round 409's own fix for this). That helper re-derives the entity list *live* from whichever checkpoints still happen to exist in the table right now -- and `deleteCheckpoint` (round 216) is a real, advertised, ordinary cleanup action ("an experimental refine that went nowhere") with zero connection to that later accounting need.

**Independent verification**: traced the concrete failure end-to-end: build a project with `Customer`+`Order` (checkpoint C1, `kind="build"`, mentions both); refine away `Order` (checkpoint C2, `kind="refine"`, mentions only `Customer`) -- `Order`'s real table survives untouched, the normal "migrated-but-orphaned" state round 409 is specifically designed to still catch via checkpoint history. Delete checkpoint C1 via the real `DELETE /projects/:id/checkpoints/:checkpointId` route (round 216) -- an entirely ordinary cleanup action, nothing about it considers `deleteProject`'s later reliance on checkpoint history. Only C2 remains, whose `spec_json` never mentions `Order` at all. Delete the whole project: `deleteProject` computes `entityNames` = current spec (`{Customer}`) ∪ `listAllCheckpointedEntityNames` (now just `{Customer}`, since C1 is gone) = `{Customer}` -- `Order`'s real table is never dropped, permanently orphaned with absolutely nothing left anywhere (project row, checkpoints, spec) still referencing it, unlike the ordinary orphan case deleteProject otherwise catches. Confirmed this is a genuinely new gap, not a repeat of round 409's own fix: round 409's fix reads whichever checkpoints exist *right now*; this gap is about a checkpoint no longer existing at all by the time `deleteProject` runs -- a cross-feature interaction between round 216 (checkpoint deletion, which only ever considered "does this affect the *current* spec") and round 409 (which came later and was never re-examined against round 216's earlier feature). Grepped `docs/roadmap.md` for related terms -- no round documents this interaction as found, deferred, or rejected.

**The fix**: added a durable, append-only ledger table, `checkpoint_entity_history` (`projectId`, `entityName`, composite primary key), created in `ensureCheckpointsTable`. `insertCheckpoint` now also writes every entity name from the checkpoint's own spec into this ledger (`INSERT OR IGNORE`) at the one point that entity name is known to be real -- so it survives that checkpoint being individually deleted later, since `deleteCheckpoint` itself is deliberately left untouched (it still only ever does a plain `DELETE FROM checkpoints`, exactly as documented). A new `listHistoricalEntityNames` reads the ledger; `deleteProject` now unions it alongside its two existing sources (current spec + `listAllCheckpointedEntityNames`) -- losing any *one* source is never by itself enough to orphan a table anymore. `deleteCheckpointsForProject` (part of `deleteProject`'s own cleanup) also clears this project's ledger rows once `deleteProject` has already read everything it needs, so the table doesn't grow forever with rows for projects that no longer exist. `ensureCheckpointsTable` backfills the ledger once from every pre-existing checkpoint's `spec_json` *and* every project's own current `spec_json` (a `UNION ALL` query, guarded to degrade gracefully if the `projects` table doesn't exist yet, e.g. in an isolated unit test) -- for data written before this ledger existed, the exact same honest-backfill discipline round 419's `kind` column migration used.

**Tests**: `packages/db/src/checkpoints.test.ts` gained four tests: `listHistoricalEntityNames` still remembers an entity name after the one checkpoint that mentioned it is deleted; it's correctly scoped per project; `deleteCheckpointsForProject` clears only its own project's ledger rows; and a dedicated backfill test standing in for a pre-existing database (raw-SQL `checkpoints`/`projects` tables with no ledger at all) confirming `ensureCheckpointsTable` backfills correctly from both sources. `packages/db/src/projects.test.ts` gained a direct repro test mirroring the existing round-409 orphan test exactly, except the one checkpoint that ever mentioned the removed entity is explicitly deleted (via the real `deleteCheckpoint`) before the project itself is deleted -- confirming the entity's real table is still dropped.

**Regression-proof**: backed up all three changed implementation files (`packages/db/src/checkpoints.ts`, `packages/db/src/projects.ts`, `packages/db/src/index.ts`) to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted all three to HEAD (keeping every updated test file). The predicted failures occurred exactly: `checkpoints.test.ts` failed as a whole-file module-load crash (`SyntaxError: ... does not provide an export named 'listHistoricalEntityNames'` -- this project's own established strong-confirmation signal for a missing export), and `projects.test.ts`'s new repro test failed on its own (112/114 passing otherwise). Restored all three files from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q` on each, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/db`/`@forge/api` suites clean (`@forge/web` confirmed to have zero dependency on `@forge/db` at all, so not re-run).

Full suite green: **127 tests** in `@forge/db` (+5), **392 tests** in `@forge/api` (unchanged -- no API-level test needed; the bug and fix are entirely inside the `@forge/db` package), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/web`, `@forge/shared`, and `@forge/spec-engine` (untouched, no re-run needed) stayed at their round-419 counts. Pushed as commit `bf31f20` + roadmap entry to follow.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. It's the same general shape round 419 named as a lesson (a value re-derived live from state an unrelated feature can mutate) applied to a different pairing: `listAllCheckpointedEntityNames`'s "whichever checkpoints exist right now" versus `deleteCheckpoint`'s "any checkpoint can be individually removed at any time," rather than round 419's "label text" versus "rename." The fix generalizes cleanly: any future feature that further prunes checkpoint history (e.g. an auto-pruning policy, round 380's still-open small candidate) will not reopen this gap, since the ledger it now feeds from is deliberately independent of which checkpoint rows still exist. Everything else still open from rounds 378-419 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 421: a role/assumption chip's remove/rename could silently act on the wrong item if two requests overlapped

**The survey**: a fresh Explore general-survey was given the full denylist through round 420 and asked to look at areas not yet covered (API routes, concurrent-request edge cases) rather than re-apply round 419/420's own "live-derived value" lesson to checkpoints again. It found that the spec review screen's roles and assumptions chips (`apps/web/src/SpecListItemRemover.tsx`'s `RoleChip`/`AssumptionItem`, added well before this round's numbering) are addressed purely by array index -- unlike entities and fields, which are addressed by their own stable `name` (immune to this). Each chip's remove/rename button captures its own `index` prop from whatever position `project.spec.roles.map((r, i) => ...)` (`App.tsx`) last rendered it at, with no global lock disabling sibling chips while one request is in flight -- only a per-chip `busy` flag.

**Independent verification**: read `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts`'s four index-addressed routes (`DELETE`/`PATCH` for both `/roles/:index` and `/assumptions/:index`) directly. Each handler re-reads the project's current spec fresh and applies its own `:index` synchronously, with no optimistic-concurrency check of any kind -- `parseListIndex` only bounds-checks the index against the list's current length. Traced the exact race: roles `["Admin", "Manager", "Member"]`; click remove on "Admin" (index 0, request A) and immediately click remove on "Manager" (index 1, request B, captured from the same original render) before request A's response lands. Request A completes first, leaving `["Manager", "Member"]`. Request B then runs with `index=1` against that already-shifted array, removing "Member" -- not "Manager", the one actually clicked -- with no error shown anywhere; the UI simply reflects whatever the last response said. The identical mechanism applies to renaming and to assumptions. Confirmed this is a structurally distinct bug class from anything in the denylist (none of those cover plain index-addressed array mutation races), and confirmed entities/fields are unaffected since `removeEntity`/`removeField`/`renameFieldLabel` all address by `name`, never by position.

**The fix**: the client (`SpecListItemRemover.tsx`) now passes `expect` -- the exact role/assumption string it had on screen when it captured `index` -- alongside every remove/rename call (`apps/web/src/api.ts`'s `removeRole`/`renameRole`/`removeAssumption`/`renameAssumption`, all gained an `expect` parameter). The server (`assertIndexStillMatches` in `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts`) checks that the list's current value at `index` still equals `expect`; if a prior overlapping request already shifted the array, it now returns `409` (`ROLE_STALE_INDEX`/`ASSUMPTION_STALE_INDEX`) instead of silently mutating a different entry. `expect` is optional server-side specifically so existing direct API callers/tests that don't send it keep working unchanged -- this app's own web client always sends it. `codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) has no roles/assumptions concept at all, confirmed by grep -- nothing to port there.

**Tests**: `apps/api/src/app.test.ts` gained four end-to-end tests: deleting a role at a now-stale index is rejected (409) while the role actually clicked survives; renaming a role at a now-stale index is rejected (409) while the role actually clicked is left untouched; the identical repro for assumption deletion; and a back-compat test confirming DELETE/PATCH without an `expect` field still succeeds unchanged. `apps/web/src/SpecListItemRemover.test.ts`'s two existing rename tests (which assert the exact PATCH request body) were updated to expect the new `expect` field alongside the renamed value.

**Regression-proof**: backed up all three changed implementation files (`apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts`, `apps/web/src/api.ts`, `apps/web/src/SpecListItemRemover.tsx`) to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted all three to HEAD (keeping every updated test file). The predicted failures occurred exactly: 3 of the 4 new API tests failed (the three asserting a 409 that the reverted code can't produce; the back-compat test correctly still passed since nothing changed for callers that omit `expect`), and both updated `SpecListItemRemover.test.ts` rename tests failed on the `expect` field being absent from the request body. Restored all three files from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q` on each, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/api`/`@forge/web` suites clean.

Full suite green: **396 tests** in `@forge/api` (+4), **808 tests** in `@forge/web` (unchanged count -- 2 existing tests updated, not added), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/db` (**127**), `@forge/shared` (**16**), and `@forge/spec-engine` (**93**) untouched, no re-run needed. Pushed as commit `f150a31` + roadmap entry to follow.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. It introduces a new general pattern distinct from round 419/420's "live-derived value/accounting" lesson: *an array addressed by bare position, rather than by a stable identifier, is fragile the moment two mutating requests against it can overlap* -- entities/fields were already immune by virtue of being name-addressed; roles/assumptions were the one remaining index-addressed pair. The fix (an optional client-supplied `expect` value, checked server-side before applying an index-based mutation) is a reusable shape for any future index-addressed list this app might add. Everything else still open from rounds 378-420 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 422: an unrelated action's refresh() during a pending delete's undo window could resurrect the deleted row (or duplicate it on Undo)

**The survey**: a fresh Explore general-survey was given the full denylist through round 421 (including round 421's own "index-addressed array" family, explicitly flagged as not re-applicable to roles/assumptions again) and asked to look at genuinely new areas -- API routes not yet audited for races, concurrent-request edge cases, other list/array mutation endpoints. It found a client-side interaction in `apps/web/src/EntityPanel.tsx`: `handleDelete`/`handleBulkDelete` optimistically remove a row from view the instant Delete is confirmed, but defer the real `DELETE` request behind a 5-second `UNDO_WINDOW_MS` window (`pendingDeleteRef`/`commitPendingDelete`, round 184/194) -- the record still genuinely exists server-side the entire time. `refresh()` (the shared "reload from server" helper) has zero awareness of `pendingDeleteRef`: it unconditionally replaces the whole `records` array with whatever `listRecords` currently returns, and is called by seven unrelated handlers -- `handleSubmit` (create/edit), `handleDuplicate`, `handleBulkDuplicate`, `handleBulkUpdate`, `handleImportFile` (CSV import), `handleMoveFields` (Kanban drag), and `commitInlineEdit` (double-click cell edit).

**Independent verification**: read `refresh()` and all seven call sites directly, confirming none of them check `pendingDeleteRef` before or after calling it. Traced the exact repro: records `[Acme Corp, Globex]`; delete Acme Corp (optimistic removal, real DELETE deferred); within the same 5s window, double-click Globex's name cell and commit an inline edit to "Globex Corp" -- `commitInlineEdit` does a real `PATCH` then `await refresh()`. Since the server still has Acme Corp (nothing told it to delete anything yet), `listRecords` returns both rows, and the unconditional `setRecords(records)` puts Acme Corp right back in the table -- with the Undo toast still showing (or already gone), and the user never having clicked Undo. The still-pending timer then fires `commitPendingDelete` for real once the window closes, genuinely deleting Acme Corp server-side -- but nothing re-renders on a successful delete (`commitPendingDelete` only calls `setRecords` on *failure*), so the row is left sitting in the table looking normal, even though it no longer exists on the server (the next click on it 404s, unexplained). Worse, if the user *does* click Undo after that resurrection, `restoreRecordAt` (which has no de-duplication of its own) splices in a second copy, producing a visible duplicate row for one underlying record. Confirmed this is a distinct bug class from the denylist's DELETE-vs-pipeline race guards and the FK-constraint-failure fix already on `commitPendingDelete` (round 292) -- this is purely refresh() vs. the undo-window mechanism, with no existing test (`EntityPanel.test.ts`) exercising "trigger refresh while a delete is still pending."

**The fix**: `refresh()` now reads `pendingDeleteRef.current?.entries` and excludes any of those record ids from what it hands to `setRecords`, regardless of which of the seven unrelated handlers triggered the call -- a record genuinely mid-undo-window stays excluded from every refresh until its own deferred DELETE (or Undo) resolves it one way or the other. `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) turned out to have the exact same `refresh()`/`pendingDeleteRef`/seven-call-site shape (ported from the live preview in earlier rounds), so the identical fix was ported there too.

**Tests**: `apps/web/src/EntityPanel.test.ts` gained two new tests: committing a real inline-cell-edit (a genuine, unrelated `refresh()` call) while another row's delete is still inside its undo window must not resurrect that row; and clicking Undo afterward must restore exactly one row, never a duplicate. The pre-existing regex-extraction test for `refresh()`'s stale-vs-fresh-refresh race (which evals the function's raw source standalone via `new Function(...)`) needed a new `pendingDeleteRef` parameter added to its injected-params list, since the fixed `refresh()` now references it -- caught immediately by the fix breaking that test with a swallowed `ReferenceError` (manifesting as "0 !== 1", the fresh refresh's own `setRecords` never firing). `apps/api/src/codegen.test.ts` gained the mirrored real-DOM test against the actual generated `EntityView` component (not a regex proxy), and its own analogous regex-extraction test for the exported app's `refresh()` got the same `pendingDeleteRef` parameter added.

**Regression-proof**: backed up both changed implementation files (`apps/web/src/EntityPanel.tsx`, `apps/api/src/codegen.ts`) to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted both to HEAD (keeping every updated test file). The predicted failures occurred: both new `EntityPanel.test.ts` tests failed (manifesting as a `waitForCondition` timeout, since the resurrected Acme Corp row shifted the flattened `<td>` indices the test's own selectors assumed), and the new `codegen.test.ts` real-DOM test failed with a direct, unambiguous assertion mismatch (`expected 'Globex Corp', actual 'Acme Corp'`) -- a strong, explicit confirmation of the exact resurrection/reordering bug. Restored both files from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q` on each, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/api`/`@forge/web` suites clean.

Full suite green: **397 tests** in `@forge/api` (+1), **810 tests** in `@forge/web` (+2), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/db` (**127**), `@forge/shared` (**16**), and `@forge/spec-engine` (**93**) untouched, no re-run needed. Pushed as commit `62b3759` + roadmap entry to follow.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. It's a new general pattern, distinct from round 421's "index-addressed array racing against overlapping mutations": *a shared "reload from server" helper that is unconditionally correct on its own can still be wrong the moment a sibling feature (an optimistic, deferred mutation with its own temporary client-side state) exists and that helper has no awareness of it* -- the bug lived entirely in the UI layer, with both the delete-undo feature and every one of the seven refresh()-calling handlers individually correct and well-tested in isolation; only their *combination* was broken. Everything else still open from rounds 378-421 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 423: account deletion never purged localStorage for projects the account merely collaborated on (plus a rejected false-positive worth recording)

**A rejected false positive first**: the first Explore survey attempt this round claimed every spec-mutating route in `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts` (`POST`/`DELETE`/`PATCH /roles`, `/assumptions`, `/entities`, `/entities/:name/fields`, `/entities/:name/label`, checkpoint-restore) has a "lost update" race: two concurrent requests could each read a stale `project.spec`, each compute their own change, and the second write clobber the first. Independent verification read every one of these handlers line by line and found **zero `await` anywhere between the read (`requireProjectAccess`/`getProject`) and the write (`updateProjectSpec`)** -- confirmed the DB driver is `node:sqlite`'s genuinely-synchronous `DatabaseSync` (`packages/db/src/connection.ts`), and the server runs as a single process with no clustering/worker_threads (`apps/api/src/server.ts`, one bare `app.listen` call). Node's single-threaded event loop cannot interleave two requests' execution when neither yields -- each request's entire synchronous handler (through its DB write and `res.json()`) runs to completion before the event loop can even begin the next one. The claimed race window simply does not exist for these routes; this is precisely the false-positive pattern an old standing lesson (rounds 356-407) already named: "race condition -- verify single process / synchronous DB before fixing." Rejected without implementing anything, and the denylist/lesson was updated to spell out *why* (no `await` between read and write = no race in this app) so a future round doesn't need to re-derive this from scratch.

**The survey (second attempt)**: re-ran Explore general-survey with the rejected finding's exact reasoning spelled out as a required check ("any race claim must point to the specific `await` creating the yield point"), and the full denylist through round 422. It found a genuine, non-concurrency gap: `apps/web/src/DeleteAccountPanel.tsx`'s effect (lines 46-54) fetches the real project list and splits it into owned vs. shared, but only ever stored the *owned* ids in state (`ownedProjectIds`) and passed only those to `onDeleted` on submit -- confirmed by `DeleteAccountPanel.test.ts`'s own existing round-403 test explicitly asserting shared ids are excluded. `App.tsx`'s `handleAccountDeleted(ownedProjectIds)` then only swept `projectPreferenceCleanup.ts`'s ~18 localStorage stores (pinned state, column widths/order, field filters, WhatsApp recent numbers, etc.) for those owned ids.

**Independent verification**: read `apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts`'s `DELETE /auth/account` handler directly -- confirmed it calls `removeAllCollaborationsForUser(db, req.userId!)` (line 197) in addition to deleting every owned project, which revokes this account's collaborator grant on every project it merely shares in. This is the exact same "this browser can never reach this project again" event round 404's own "leave project" fix (`App.tsx`'s `CollaboratorsPanel` `onLeft` callback) already recognized needs a `purgeProjectPreferences` sweep for a *single* project -- just never retrofitted into the account-deletion path for the (potentially many) shared projects implicitly "left" as a side effect of deleting the whole account. Traced the repro: User B collaborates on User A's Project X, pins it, resizes a column, sets a filter, sends a WhatsApp test message (each stored in User B's own browser, keyed by Project X's id); User B deletes their account; the server revokes B's access to X but `handleAccountDeleted` never receives X's id since B never owned it; every one of Project X's ~18 localStorage entries sits in User B's browser forever. Confirmed this is a distinct gap from the denylist's existing "account-deletion/leave-project preference-purge" closures: round 403 covered owned-project purge on account deletion, round 404 covered single-project purge on leaving one project by itself -- neither covered account deletion's own implicit mass "leave" of every shared project at once.

**The fix**: `DeleteAccountPanel` now also collects `sharedProjectIds` (`projects.filter(p => p.ownerId !== userId)`) alongside the existing `ownedProjectIds`, and `onDeleted`'s signature grew a second parameter to carry them. `App.tsx`'s `handleAccountDeleted(ownedProjectIds, sharedProjectIds)` now purges both arrays. `codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) has no auth/account-deletion concept at all, confirmed by grep -- nothing to port there.

**Tests**: `DeleteAccountPanel.test.ts`'s existing round-403 test was split into two: one confirming `onDeleted`'s first argument is still exactly the owned ids, and a new one confirming the second argument is exactly the shared ids (`p3`, owned by "someone-else"), excluding any owned one. `App.test.ts`'s existing regex-extraction test for `handleAccountDeleted` (which evals the function's raw source via `new Function(...)`) was updated for the new two-parameter signature and now asserts purge calls cover both owned and shared ids, in order; its "none owned" edge case was extended to "none owned and none shared."

**Regression-proof**: backed up both changed implementation files (`apps/web/src/App.tsx`, `apps/web/src/DeleteAccountPanel.tsx`) to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted both to HEAD (keeping every updated test file). The predicted failures occurred exactly: the regex-extraction test failed outright with "expected to find handleAccountDeleted in App.tsx" (its new two-parameter signature regex couldn't match the reverted one-parameter function), and the new "second argument is shared ids" test failed with `actual: undefined` (the reverted `onDeleted` call only ever passes one argument) -- while the three other, unrelated tests in the same files correctly kept passing, confirming the revert didn't touch anything else. Restored both files from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q` on each, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/web` suite clean.

Full suite green: **811 tests** in `@forge/web` (+1), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/db` (**127**), `@forge/shared` (**16**), `@forge/spec-engine` (**93**), and `@forge/api` (**397**, untouched by this round's web-only fix) stayed at their round-422 counts. Pushed as commit `9f9f55f` + roadmap entry to follow.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. It completes the "preference-purge on every real access-loss event" family the denylist already tracked (389/390/403/404/405) with the one remaining convergent path: account deletion's own implicit mass revocation of shared-project access, previously only handled for the account's *owned* projects. The rejected false positive is recorded here deliberately, not discarded, since an incorrect "fix" for a non-existent race would have been pure wasted churn (and risked confusing a future round into thinking the pattern was already closed when it was never real to begin with) -- the next round's survey denylist/lessons should treat "a route handler with literally zero `await` between its read and its write" as conclusively race-free in this specific single-process, synchronous-SQLite app, not as a candidate needing its own investigation each time. Everything else still open from rounds 378-422 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 424: account deletion could orphan a brand-new project created during the slow WhatsApp-disconnect window

**The survey**: with round 423's "a race claim must point to the specific `await` creating the yield point" requirement spelled out explicitly, and the full denylist through round 423, Explore general-survey found a genuine race in `apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts`'s `DELETE /auth/account` handler -- distinct from round 423's rejected false positive because this one names a real, confirmed yield point. The handler's per-project cleanup loop does `await whatsapp.disconnect(projectId).catch(() => {})` for every project this account owns, and `deleteAllSessionsForUser` (which revokes the token making this very request) only ran *after* that whole loop finished.

**Independent verification**: read `WhatsAppWebManager.disconnect()` (`apps/api/src/whatsappWeb.ts:363-379`) directly -- when a project has a live WhatsApp session, it does `await session.sock.logout().catch(() => {})`, a genuine Baileys socket call that performs real network I/O against WhatsApp's own servers, not an instantly-resolving promise -- confirmed this is a real yield point, the same class the round-423 lesson explicitly allows ("a WhatsApp socket operation"). While the account-deletion request is suspended there, the token making it is still valid (sessions aren't revoked until after the loop), so an unrelated `POST /projects` (`apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts:358-376`, itself doing a real `await generateSpec(...)` call) using that same token can run to completion and `insertProject` a brand-new project. That new project's id was never in the `listOwnedProjectIds` snapshot taken once, up front, so it's never passed to `deleteProject`. Confirmed `packages/db/src/projects.ts`'s own `CREATE TABLE projects` has no `ownerId REFERENCES users(id)` foreign key at all, so the subsequent unconditional `deleteUser(db, req.userId!)` (`packages/db/src/users.ts:141-143`, a bare `DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ?`) still succeeds -- permanently orphaning the new project under a user id that no longer exists anywhere, reachable by no route ever again (no login, no session, no admin sweep path). Confirmed this is distinct from round 411's fix (which closed a *different* orphaning mechanism -- `listProjectsForUser`'s tolerant spec-parsing silently excluding an *already-existing* project from the snapshot) and from round 379's WhatsApp disconnect/connect race (which was about `disconnect()` racing a still-in-flight `connect()` inside `whatsappWeb.ts` itself, unrelated to account-deletion's own project enumeration).

**The fix**: moved `deleteAllSessionsForUser(db, req.userId!)` to run first, synchronously, as the very first statement in the handler's try block -- before `listOwnedProjectIds` and before the WhatsApp-disconnect loop's own real I/O. Any request racing this one (using the same token) now fails `requireAuth` immediately instead of racing a live multi-await window, for the same reason the route's own existing test already expects ("the deleted user's own session token must stop working immediately"). `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) has no auth/account-deletion concept at all, confirmed by grep -- nothing to port there.

**Tests**: `apps/api/src/app.test.ts` gained one new end-to-end test that deterministically forces the exact window open -- holds the fake WhatsApp socket's own `logout()` call open with a real, manually-released promise (the same hold-the-async-call-open technique used elsewhere in this file, rather than a timing-based sleep), fires `DELETE /auth/account`, waits for `logout()` to actually be entered, then fires a racing `POST /projects` with the same token and asserts it's rejected (401) before releasing the held `logout()` and confirming the deletion itself still completes (204).

**Regression-proof**: backed up the one changed implementation file (`apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts`) to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted it to HEAD (keeping the updated test file). The predicted failure occurred exactly: the new test failed with `expected: 401, actual: 201` -- the racing `POST /projects` succeeded and created a real project while the reverted handler was still suspended inside the WhatsApp disconnect, a direct, unambiguous confirmation of the exact vulnerability. Restored the file from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q`, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/api` suite clean.

Full suite green: **398 tests** in `@forge/api` (+1), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/db` (**127**), `@forge/shared` (**16**), `@forge/spec-engine` (**93**), and `@forge/web` (**811**, untouched by this round's API-only fix) stayed at their round-423 counts. Pushed as commit `699fe7c` + roadmap entry to follow.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. Together with round 423's rejected false positive, this round validates the exact boundary the new lesson draws: a route handler with zero `await` between read and write is conclusively race-free in this single-process app (round 423's correct rejection), while a route handler with a real, named `await` performing genuine I/O (AI provider calls, WhatsApp socket operations, `setTimeout`-based deferrals) is a legitimate race candidate worth investigating on its own mechanical terms (this round's correct acceptance). The general fix shape -- revoke access/invalidate the actor *before* starting any slow, multi-await cleanup cascade, rather than after -- is reusable for any future route that mixes real async I/O with a security-relevant state change. Everything else still open from rounds 378-423 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 425: five real server error codes had no Hebrew (or English) translation, leaking raw English text into the Hebrew-first UI -- plus the self-maintaining completeness test that was supposed to catch this had its own blind spots

**The survey**: Explore general-survey, working from the round-424 denylist, found that `apps/web/src/i18n/language.ts`'s dictionary was missing entries for five real, currently-thrown server error codes: `ROLE_NOT_FOUND`, `ASSUMPTION_NOT_FOUND`, `ROLE_STALE_INDEX`, `ASSUMPTION_STALE_INDEX` (all four thrown by `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts`'s `parseListIndex`/`assertIndexStillMatches` helpers, the latter two being round 421's own additions), and `INVALID_RELATION_TARGET` (thrown by the record create/update routes' FK-violation translation). `resolveErrorMessage()`'s fallback chain (`apps/web/src/i18n/language.ts`) means a code missing from *both* dictionaries falls through to the server's raw English `body.error` string, verbatim, in an otherwise fully Hebrew-localized UI.

**Independent verification**: `grep`'d every one of the five codes' exact throw/call sites in `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts` (lines ~1007-1011, 1173-1174, 1192-1197, 1223-1224, 1243-1248, 1468-1472) and confirmed none had a matching `error.*` key in either language block of `language.ts`. Cross-checked completeness the other direction too: extracted every ALL-CAPS string literal across `apps/api/src` via a broad grep, filtered out SQL keywords and non-codes by hand, and diffed the result against the dictionary's existing `error.*` keys -- confirmed exactly these five, and no others, were missing.

While verifying with the project's own pre-existing dynamic completeness test (`apps/web/src/i18n/language.test.ts`'s `findThrownHttpErrorCodes()`, which regex-scans the real `apps/api/src` source instead of checking a hand-maintained list -- built specifically because a hand-maintained list had already silently missed `ALREADY_BUILT`/`PIPELINE_IN_PROGRESS` once before), found the scanner itself has two genuine blind spots that let exactly this round's bug through undetected: its regex, `new HttpError\(\s*\d+\s*,[\s\S]*?"([A-Z_]+)"\s*\)`, required the code string to sit with *no* trailing comma directly before the call's closing `)` -- `INVALID_RELATION_TARGET`'s own call site is formatted multi-line with a trailing comma (`"INVALID_RELATION_TARGET",\n  );`), so the scanner never saw it. And `parseListIndex`/`assertIndexStillMatches` take their HttpError code as a `notFoundCode` *parameter*, not a literal string inside their own `new HttpError(...)` calls -- the literal only ever appears at each *call site* -- so no amount of tolerating formatting in the original pattern could ever have found `ROLE_NOT_FOUND`/`ASSUMPTION_NOT_FOUND`/`ROLE_STALE_INDEX`/`ASSUMPTION_STALE_INDEX` at all. Confirmed both blind spots empirically: after fixing only the dictionary and leaving the scanner as-is, test #17 ("every HttpError code the API can send has a Hebrew and an English translation") passed *regardless* of whether the dictionary fix was present, because the scanner's own output never included any of the five codes to check against -- meaning the existing safety net would have given a false "all clear" both before and after the real fix, and would let the same bug class recur silently in the future.

**The fix**: two parts. (1) Added the five missing keys to both the Hebrew and English blocks of `apps/web/src/i18n/language.ts`, positioned after the existing `error.RECORD_HAS_DEPENDENT_RECORDS` entries in each. (2) Strengthened `findThrownHttpErrorCodes()` in `apps/web/src/i18n/language.test.ts` itself: the main pattern now tolerates an optional trailing comma (`"([A-Z_]+)"\s*,?\s*\)`), and a second pattern (`delegatedCodePattern`) specifically scans call sites of `parseListIndex`/`assertIndexStillMatches` for their literal last-argument code string, since those can never appear next to `new HttpError(` itself. `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) has no i18n/translation infrastructure at all, confirmed by grep -- nothing to port there.

**Tests**: strengthened the existing "sanity check on the scan itself" test (`apps/web/src/i18n/language.test.ts`) to also assert the scanner finds `INVALID_RELATION_TARGET` (the trailing-comma case) and `ROLE_NOT_FOUND`/`ASSUMPTION_STALE_INDEX` (the delegated-parameter case), rather than adding a separate new test -- this directly exercises and proves the fixed scanner's own coverage, which is what actually regression-proofs this bug class going forward (a hand-written test asserting five specific translations exist would not have caught the scanner's blind spots that let this round's bug ship in the first place).

**Regression-proof**: backed up both changed files (`language.ts`, `language.test.ts`) to the session scratchpad. Reverted only `language.ts` (keeping the fixed scanner) and reran the suite: test #17 failed exactly as predicted (`missing Hebrew translation for error.ROLE_NOT_FOUND`), the first time this safety net has actually been proven to catch this bug class rather than silently passing either way. Restored `language.ts` from backup, confirmed both files byte-identical via `diff -q`, then reran the full monorepo build and both full suites clean.

Full suite green: **20/20** in `apps/web/src/i18n/language.test.ts` (including the two strengthened scanner-sanity assertions), **398 tests** in `@forge/api` (untouched, no API changes this round), full monorepo `npm run build` clean. `@forge/web`'s full suite reran clean at its existing count (web-only i18n change, no new test added beyond the scanner-sanity strengthening). `@forge/db` (**127**), `@forge/shared` (**16**), `@forge/spec-engine` (**93**) stayed at their round-424 counts.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed, and it's a new case shape for this routine worth naming: the bug wasn't just missing data (five translations), it was a hole in the *detector* that's specifically supposed to prevent missing translations from shipping silently -- discovered only by actually reasoning through the scanner's own regex against the real call-site formatting, not by trusting its "all tests pass" output at face value. The general lesson: when a fix is verified by an existing automated check, independently confirm that check would actually have failed *before* the fix (not just that it passes after) -- a check that passes either way is not evidence of anything. Everything else still open from rounds 378-424 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 426: an entity named exactly "WhatsApp Messages" could silently destroy a whole dataset on "Backup all data"

**The survey**: Explore general-survey, working from the full round-425 denylist (including the fresh instruction to also check other automated scanners for similar blind spots), found that `apps/api/src/backup.ts`'s `generateBackupZipEntries` builds one ZIP entry per entity at `` `${sanitizeZipEntryName(entity.name)}.csv` ``, then unconditionally pushes a second entry at the hardcoded literal path `"WhatsApp Messages.csv"` whenever the project has any WhatsApp message history -- with no check against the entity-derived paths already queued.

**Independent verification**: read `backup.ts` directly and confirmed lines 187-198 exactly as described: the entity-derived entries are built first, then the hardcoded WhatsApp-log entry is pushed with a bare string literal, no collision check at all. Confirmed `sanitizeZipEntryName("WhatsApp Messages") === "WhatsApp Messages"` (it only replaces path separators and control characters, never spaces -- deliberately, per round 285's own comment, so a human-readable Hebrew/English entity name stays readable in the archive listing) and `apps/api/src/zip.ts`'s `buildZip` does zero deduplication on `entry.path` (confirmed by reading it end to end -- it just serializes whatever `entries` array it's given). So a project with an entity named exactly `"WhatsApp Messages"` produces two ZIP entries at the identical path, and every common unzip tool (Info-ZIP, Windows Explorer, macOS Archive Utility) resolves that by extracting them in archive order and letting the later one overwrite the earlier one on disk -- a whole dataset lost, with no error or warning anywhere. Confirmed this is reachable in practice, not purely theoretical: `ProductSpecSchema` (`packages/shared/src/index.ts`) has no ASCII-identifier restriction on entity `name` at all (an earlier round deliberately rejected adding one -- "EntitySchema ASCII restriction" is on this routine's own out-of-scope list) and no reservation for this specific string (unlike `id`/`createdAt` via `RESERVED_FIELD_NAMES`), so an AI-generated spec for an app that itself prominently features a WhatsApp integration producing that exact wording in `name` passes validation cleanly and reaches a real, built project. `findCaseInsensitiveDuplicateEntityNames`/`findSanitizedIdentifierCollisions` (same file) only ever compare entity names against *each other*, never against this hardcoded literal that lives only inside `backup.ts` -- so nothing anywhere in the spec-validation pipeline could have caught this. Confirmed it's not a race: `generateBackupZipEntries` is entirely synchronous string/array building, with zero `await` anywhere in it.

Also checked `apps/api/src/codegen.ts`'s own exported-app `/api/backup` route (same `${entity.name}.csv` pattern, confirmed by reading it) for an equivalent fix: not needed, for two independent reasons. First, the exported standalone app has no WhatsApp integration at all, so there's no hardcoded log entry there to collide with in the first place. Second, round 285's own roadmap entry already verified (and this round re-confirmed by reading `generateExportFiles`) that every entity reaching the exported app has already passed `assertSafe(entity.name, "entity")`, which *rejects* any non-ASCII-identifier name outright -- strictly safer than `sanitizeZipEntryName`'s sanitize-only approach, and a space-containing name like `"WhatsApp Messages"` fails that check before export ever happens.

**The fix**: added `uniqueWhatsAppLogPath()` to `backup.ts` -- after the entity-derived entries are built, it checks (case-insensitively, matching the rest of this codebase's naming-conflict convention) whether `"WhatsApp Messages.csv"` already exists among them, and if so, resolves the collision with the exact same deterministic numeric-suffix loop `deriveEntityName`/`deriveFieldName` (`apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts`) already use for every other naming conflict in this codebase (`"WhatsApp Messages 2.csv"`, `3`, ... until free). The entity keeps its own real, user-facing name untouched; the hardcoded log entry is the one that yields.

**Tests**: `apps/api/src/backup.test.ts` gained one new test -- builds a project with both a real entity named exactly `"WhatsApp Messages"` (holding its own real record) and real WhatsApp message history, confirms every resulting ZIP entry path is unique (`new Set(paths).size === paths.length`), confirms the entity keeps the literal path `"WhatsApp Messages.csv"` with its own real record's content, and confirms the real WhatsApp log still exists in the archive under some other unique path, rather than being silently dropped.

**Regression-proof**: backed up `backup.ts` to the session scratchpad, `git checkout --` reverted it to HEAD (keeping the new test). The predicted failure occurred exactly: `"no two ZIP entries may share the same path" -- 3 !== 4` -- the exact collision this fix prevents, reproduced on demand. Restored the file from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff -q`, then reran the full monorepo build and the full `@forge/api` suite clean.

Full suite green: **399 tests** in `@forge/api` (+1), plus a clean full monorepo `npm run build`. `@forge/db` (**127**), `@forge/shared` (**16**), `@forge/spec-engine` (**93**), and `@forge/web` (**811**, untouched -- this round's fix is API-only) stayed at their round-425 counts. Pushed as commit `2c0f69e`.

**Topic status**: this fix is closed. It's a sibling of round 285's own path-safety fix in the same file and function, but a genuinely distinct mechanism: round 285 was about an *unsafe character* (a path separator) in a user-controlled name reaching an unguarded ZIP path; this round is about a user-controlled name colliding with an *unrelated hardcoded literal* that the user-controlled naming space was never checked against at all. The general lesson for any future hardcoded identifier mixed into a space otherwise populated by free-form user/AI-generated names: check for collision against that literal specifically, don't assume the existing user-name validation (schema rejection, case-collision checks between user names) has any awareness of it. Everything else still open from rounds 378-425 remains open and unchanged.

### Round 430: ICS calendar export line-folding counted UTF-16 units, not UTF-8 octets -- broken for this app's own primary language, Hebrew

**The survey**: Explore general-survey, prompted to look both for fresh ground and for other hardcoded-literal/collision-prone spots (round 426's own fresh lesson) and other self-checking scanners with blind spots (round 425's), independently re-derived a gap that had actually been sitting on this routine's own "small open candidates" list since round 367 as `` `calendarIcs.ts`'s UTF-16-vs-UTF-8 fold `` -- flagged repeatedly across dozens of subsequent rounds' closing candidate lists, never implemented. `apps/web/src/calendarIcs.ts`'s `foldIcsLine` (and its byte-for-byte duplicate in `apps/api/src/codegen.ts`, the exported app's own ICS export) checked `line.length <= 75` to decide whether RFC 5545 §3.1's 75-*octet* line-fold limit applied -- `.length` counts UTF-16 code units (characters, for Hebrew's BMP range), not bytes of the line's UTF-8 encoding.

**Independent verification**: confirmed `foldIcsLine`'s exact logic in both files, and that `buildCalendarIcs`'s `DESCRIPTION` is built from real field labels/values via `` `${f.label ?? f.name}: ${value}` `` -- exactly the Hebrew business data (e.g. "לקוח: דנה לוי") this Hebrew-primary app actually generates. A Hebrew character is 1 UTF-16 unit but 2 UTF-8 bytes, so a line of up to 75 Hebrew characters (up to 150 real bytes) passed the `<= 75` check as if compliant, and even a line long enough to trigger folding got chopped into chunks of 75 *characters* = 150 *bytes* each -- still double the limit. Confirmed the existing test (`calendarIcs.test.ts`'s fold test, using `"x".repeat(120)` -- pure ASCII) never exercised this at all, since for ASCII 1 character *is* 1 byte; the gap was invisible to its own regression-proofing by construction, the same shape of self-checking blind spot round 425 found in the i18n scanner. `git log --all -S foldIcsLine` confirmed no commit since the original round 264/265 feature had ever touched the folding-unit logic.

**The fix**: both `calendarIcs.ts` and `codegen.ts`'s `foldIcsLine` now measure real UTF-8 byte length via `TextEncoder` (not `Buffer`, which doesn't exist in `calendarIcs.ts`'s actual browser runtime) and split on whole characters (`Array.from`, never a raw index, so a surrogate pair is never torn in half) while tracking a byte budget instead of a character count. Writing the Hebrew regression test surfaced a *second*, character-set-independent bug in the same function: RFC 5545's continuation-line format prepends a single space to every folded line after the first, so a chunk sized to exactly 75 bytes printed as a 76-byte physical line once that space was added -- a pure off-by-one present even for ASCII content, never caught because the original test only ever checked the *first* folded line's length, not every continuation line. Fixed by giving the first chunk a 75-byte budget and every continuation chunk a 74-byte budget (leaving room for its own leading space). Updated `apps/api/src/codegen.test.ts`'s regex-extraction tests to also pull in the new `utf8ByteLength` helper `foldIcsLine` now calls, since the dynamically-assembled test function would otherwise throw `utf8ByteLength is not defined` the instant folding actually ran.

**Tests**: strengthened the existing ASCII fold test in `calendarIcs.test.ts` to assert real UTF-8 byte length rather than `.length` (coincidentally identical for ASCII, so this alone wouldn't have caught the bug -- the point is making the assertion measure the right thing going forward). Added a dedicated new test building a Hebrew `DESCRIPTION` whose character count looks RFC-compliant but whose real UTF-8 byte count does not, asserting every folded physical line (not just the first) stays within the 75-octet budget.
